title: Wardogs is hitting 185,000 accounts with a ban wave as Season 3 lands
author: Vikki Blake
content:
Ruff justice.

Wardogs' Season 3 will launch on 12th November, complete with a new urban map, a new Limited Mode, and a ban wave targeting 185,000 accounts.

Developer Bulkhead confirmed the details earlier this week, revealing plans for a full wipe and progression changes that it hopes will "recapture the shared discovery and sense of achievement that defined" the 100-player tactical shooter when it first launched in Early Access.

The new map will focus on close-quarters fighting, and for a "more level playing field", players can dip into Limited Mode, which offers "an alternative way to experience" the game as it restricts weapons, ammunition, armour, and vehicles.

While the full list of restrictions is still being decided, it currently includes FMJ-only ammunition, a Tier 2 armour cap, and a reduced attack vehicle selection.

"The mode is designed to preserve the feel of early-to-mid-game combat and reduce the advantage offered by more powerful equipment," the team said.

Bulkhead also confirmed seasons are getting longer. From now on, they’ll last three months, giving players "more time to work towards their goals before each wipe and the development team more time to prepare future updates". Progression will also be "brought closer to the pace of Season 1", following the studio’s acknowledgement that Season 2 accelerated "the journey too aggressively".

"Season 3 is about giving players a new battlefield to learn together and a progression journey worth spending time on," said Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer. "Longer seasons give everyone more room to reach their own goals, and give us the time to properly develop what comes next."

Alongside Season 3, Bulkhead revealed it has used machine learning to review is "activating further layers of its anti-cheat" after analysing 187 million hours of gameplay with help from machine learning. It says having close to four million unique players since launch gave it enough data to pull that work forward from next year.

"[E]xploiters, real-money traders, and gold-farming networks" have been permanently banned and lost their server-hosting privileges, and a player trust score is planned for 2027.

"Protecting the people who play Wardogs fairly is essential to everything we're building," Brammer added.

Bigger changes to the metagame, including a new progression system, are also due in 2027 as Bulkhead works towards Wardogs 1.0. Full Season 3 patch notes will be out before launch.

Wardogs launched in Steam Early Access on 10th September, and is due on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S in 2028.

Wardogs is one of the breakout successes of the year. In our early access Wardogs review, we said the game's mix of competitive shooters' best bits with something entirely of its own made it "a brilliantly refreshing take on the genre".

title: AMD has patched its SSD-eating GPU driver bug with an optional Adrenalin update for RX 7000-series graphics cards and above
author: Andy Edser
content:
I reported earlier this week on a bug within AMD's GPU driver suite, wherein a misfiring utility was accused of making huge amounts of erroneous storage writes. Some AMD graphics card owners reported their SSD health dropping by up to 1% per month, but a fix has finally arrived.

AMD Adrenalin Edition 26.11.1 is an optional update, which means you'll need to download the installer yourself. However, according to the topline notes, the update fixes "excessive writes to the system drive" at idle for Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards and above.

AMD's wording suggests that older GPUs might not be affected by the bug, but some of the user reports mention RX 6000-series cards, so it's unclear if a fix for earlier models is still in the works.

I also think it's a slightly odd move to make this an "optional" update, given the severity of some of the reports, though this is often how AMD deals with getting fixes out in between official driver releases—by the looks of the known issues, this interim driver might still need some work before it's patched into the next full release.

AMD lists a litany of potential issues with various games, including crashes and driver timeouts in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, War Thunder, and Cyberpunk 2077 with FSR enabled. These issues, however, match and are fewer than in the previous driver release, with the exception of the Phantom Blade Zero bug.

The company notes that "visual corruption may appear on character hair while playing Phantom Blade Zero on Radeon RX 9000 series graphics products." I'm currently working my way through PBZ myself, and the idea of turning down the quality settings on Soul's magnificent hairdo? Sacrilege, as far as I'm concerned.

Still, I'd definitely consider downloading the update if my SSD health was rapidly being eaten by a misfiring utility. Buying a replacement these days isn't cheap, so anything that prevents unnecessary wear and tear on existing hardware is a-okay with me.

Andy built his first gaming PC at the tender age of 12, when IDE cables were a thing and high resolution wasn't. 26 years later (yes he's getting old), he now spends his days writing about and reviewing graphics cards, CPUs, keyboards, mice, gaming headsets and much, much more. You name it, if it's PC gaming hardware he'll write words about it, with opinions and everything.

title: Vice City was the GTA that established Rockstar's killer formula - and 24 years on, it's still one of the best games ever made
author: Dom Peppiatt
content:
"Get the limey out of here," Burt Reynolds tells the producers of GTA: Vice City during a recording session for the game, as Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser enters the studio. "I'm not going to work if this limey Brit is in here!" Houser refuses to leave, so the story goes - he just came down to meet one of his heroes! - and he and Reynolds end up chest-to-chest, about to come to blows, before a studio engineer breaks up the fight.

I can't verify the truth of this story. It's one of those development rumours that's been around for a long time, originally written in a book about how games conquered pop culture called "All Your Base Are Belong to Us" by Harold Goldberg. But I like to believe it's true, because in this one moment, the two crucial strands of GTA: Vice City's DNA helix together: its star power and Rockstar's arrogance.

And I'm not saying that in a pejorative way at all. I think a game of Vice City's scope - stretched to breaking with ambition, budget, and technical wizardry - couldn't exist without the ego trip of Rockstar at its highest. This is a game that (somehow!) started as a bit of DLC for GTA 3, supposedly intended to launch as a mission pack when Rockstar North figured out how to port it to PC. GTA 3 launched in October 2001, and by some miracle - and lots of crunch, no doubt - Vice City hit shelves in October 2002.

This game - a game that would come to represent everything the GTA series is, for generations to come - was put together in about a year. I'd feel pretty full of myself, too, if I was able to crank out that sort of quality in that sort of timeframe. With a development budget of approximately $5 million (massive at the time, even though it seems paltry against GTA 6's rumoured $1 billion+) and a marketing spend of $13.2 million, Vice City's budget was indicative of a series shifting toward becoming a cultural milestone - a standard bearer for video games as a whole, and as explosive and attention-grabbing as Hollywood's biggest events.

It's not like Rockstar needed to borrow credibility from the movie industry to inject some panache into its work, but even so, I think it's in its vortex of unbelievable Hollywood talent that Vice City really makes its mark. This was the first time Rockstar used a voiced protagonist, and by the developer's own admission, it was "a riddle" they had to solve. It didn't come easy; by making the protagonist a fullyfleshed-out character, players also had to like him - not an easy ask when he's a bonafide psychopath with a fetish for revenge like Tommy Vercetti. But Ray Liotta pulls it off without breaking a sweat. The actor has gone on record saying it was a rough gig ("You're creating a character that's not there before", he bizarrely complained in one interview), and Vice City director Navid Khonsari often moaned about the actor's unpredictable moods, so I imagine the mood in the booth wasn't great, but the result? The result is phenomenal.

You shouldn't like Vercetti. He's arrogant, he's brash, he's a totem for all the worst elements of misogynistic 80s excess. And yet, because he's such a cartoon caricature of a Miami gangster, he becomes a sort of quasi-romantic figure; a mob stooge who's been set up by his old 'business associates' and by the very fabric of the American Dream. Vice City is, in a sense, a redemption story dressed in the clothes of a revenge one. Vercetti dreams of being a self-made man, of taming this new frontier of unbridled capitalism and clawing back the years that were taken from him by the mob in Liberty City.

From the moment he arrives in town and a cocaine deal quickly goes south, Vercetti is on the back foot. In the opening hours of the game, he - and, of course, you by extension - work for pocket change, picking up menial jobs here and there while meeting all the freaks and strangers Vice City has to offer. There are no less than 50 story characters here, brought to life by Ray Liotta, Tom Sizemore, Luis Guzmán, Gary Busey, Danny Trejo, Debbie Harry, Danny Dyer, Philip Michael Thomas, William Fichtner, and many, many more besides.

1 of 6

Caption

Attribution

Playing Vice City again in 2026, I was absolutely floored by this cast - and how well their personalities and mannerisms translate to the almost puppet-like visuals Rockstar deployed for the game. Reynolds - despite not having a good time in the booth, if the story up top is anything to go by - is a highlight; the bombast and bravado of his Avery Carrington feels like a prototype for some of the more extreme characters we meet later in the series. I think I can even see a bit of Trevor in him, you know? It's how the Housers would take a trope - say, ruthless Texan oil magnate - and amplify it to its furthest, most cartoon extreme: what does this person look like with all the guardrails off, with the heady intoxication of unlimited capital at their disposal? For Trevor, that trope is 'unhinged redneck' and the cartoonish extreme is 'without a single shred of a conscience'. You can apply the formula to just about anything in the series, and it makes sense.

For Tommy Vercetti, though, it's slightly more nuanced. He isn't just 'Scarface' with a touch more humanity - no, he's a tragic figure, betrayed by all his closest friends. In striving to take back some power and gain a little more control over his life, he ends up decapitating the local drug smuggling scene and taking over as its head. The first half of Vice City is Sisyphean; an endless, uphill slog to scrabble just enough money to get by. Then, all of a sudden, the world opens up: you're now head of a drug smuggling ring, operating out of a suspiciously Scarface-like mansion, with the city at your fingertips.

The way the game, previously tightly-coiled and a bit miserly with its freedom, now unfurls in front of you is a perfect reflection of this new-found power. Suddenly, your world isn't governed by the little mission icons on your minimap, you're not being told what to do over the phone by contacts wanting something from you. No, you're calling the shots. This is the 80s, so those that are making it big are making it big, and those that are failing are failing. In a breathless display of uber-capitalist Yuppie thinking, you can even buy out nearly-bankrupt businesses and run them to your liking. The strategy is two-fold: one, you gain fronts for your other illicit activities, and two, you diversify your income streams and safeguard your assets should any one element fail.

And it's here, in its glorious second half, that Vice City becomes a breezy, beautiful bit of open-world catnip that fuses gameplay and story in a way few games have done so successfully since. You can buy a strip club (where you can launder cash), the Malibu Club (which comes with an outlandish set of missions culminating in a heist), the Cherry Popper ice cream van company (a front for dealing), the boatyard (a drug smuggling base run by two excellent potheads), Sunshine Autos (a fence for stolen cars), Kaufman Cabs (headed up by an old controller played by Debbie Harry), Interglobal Studios (an adult movie production company), and the Print Works (a counterfeiting operation). The roleplaying as Vercetti takes off; you're a bigshot touring his empire, helping out here and there, meeting your crew, setting up deals. This should feel like drudgery; workaday tedium unbecoming for a legitimate businessman like yourself. But every job, every bit of flavour text and dialogue, feeds into your growing sense of power… and Vercetti's unstoppable ego.

Alongside these key story beats are Vice City's non-essential tasks - which feel like a precursor to the 'Strangers and Freaks' missions in later GTA and Red Dead games - including the Love Fist missions. These, I think, are the best missions in the game (I'd also like to note here that 'Jez Torrent' is an amazing name for a New Wave of British Heavy metal frontman). But it's the way these core and non-essential missions dovetail that feels so great, and where the open world of Vice City really comes into its own.

In many ways, Rockstar's work here created the blueprint for what would become the Grand Theft Auto 'formula'; galvanising cinematic setpieces with free-roam activities and meta-progression that manage to alloy player agency with this sense of perpetual, unstoppable momentum. And it's all fun, too. There are some abysmal tasks, sure - piloting RC aircraft to ruin building sites, navigating boats with the wonkiest physics you've ever seen around stunt courses, waiting 15 minutes a pop for rare cars to spawn - but generally speaking, Vice City has the fun factor.

I don't think that's something I can say of other GTA games: I think often, they're a bit bloated around the middle, padded out with baggy missions and feckless busywork to give the illusion of depth and breadth. GTA 4 is also one of the most dour and oppressive open worlds I've experienced (this is a compliment, mostly), but it's not particularly fun. GTA 5, especially the Trevor segments out in the rural counties, can get a bit one-note - why introduce us to this massive world, to the state of Los Santos, if you're going to quarantine us to the rural outskirts when we're just starting to familiarise ourselves with the city? Why put up rails in a world begging us to revel in its open-ended sandbox? The only time that happens in Vice City is at the start, and the game is better for it: 'if you want to live the Scarface fantasy, buddy, you've got to earn it'.

And there's so much to love about the vibes of Vice City. The guys in shorts smoking pot on the beach; the girls in bikinis rollerblading down the promenade; the neon-drenched slick of a Florida night in the rain; the still-unbelievable who's who of music, deployed with panache in certain cutscenes; the incidental chatter of coked-up presenters on the radio; the distinct realisation of the Haitian and Cuban districts on the map; how 'downtown' actually feels like downtown. You'd think all this would have aged out of relevance by now - especially with GTA 5 being as lush and premium as it is - so it's a real credit to all those Rockstar employees that no doubt spent countless nights sleeping under their desks that Vice City still feels this good now, in 2026.

GTA: Vice City is still one of the best games ever made, I think, and probably one of the most important, too. Buoyed by Rockstar's ambition, and propelled to mainstream success by the strength of its cast, it represented video games coming out of their awkward teenage years and blossoming into young adults; biting off slightly more than they could chew, but cocksure and confident all at the same time.

Given how much of Vice City is built around the visibility and power of its cast, it's disappointing we're never going to see these characters really represented in any other GTA title again. Liotta, already unhappy about the process of recording his lines, reportedly refused to come back as Vercetti for San Andreas. And that's a real shame because - by former lead writer Dan Houser's own admission - Liotta saved his "awful writing" with his talent. The actor passed away in May 2022.

Though he balked with Reynolds, Vice City director Khonsari could usually corral the rampant ego of his Hollywood hires in the GTA studio. "If you want me to break it down to you," he’d say, "these games gross over half a billion dollars, more than all of your movies put together!" I think you can see that bravado in the spirit of Vice City, and reflected in the runaway ego of Tommy Vercetti. And I think - without that almost toxic sense of self-belief - Vice City would never have happened.

title: Forage and fight for ingredients in a magical 1960s Italy and whip up some tasty meals Cooking Mama style in The Snackbar at the End of the World
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
That's a spicy meatball

If a game is about cooking, at minimum I'll have to give it a quick testspin. Outside of this whole writing about video games thing, my other lot in life is soul bound to food, so I'm always curious to see how the two can be mixed together. And earlier this week, The Snackbar at the End of the World was revealed, a wonderfully cartoonish action-adventure game set in a magical, slightly post-apocalyptic version of 1960s Italy where you go out and forage for ingredients while fending off monstrous crops before turning them into tasty meals back in your struggling restaurant.

First up, I just have to gush over the artstyle a bit. The whole game is hand-drawn with a colourful, comic book look that has an impressive sense of depth to it. It gives off a deep love of Italian architecture and landscapes, and that admiration clearly extends to the food too. Once you've gotten the ingredients you need, you then, loosely in the vein of Cooking Mama, prepare them and make various classic Italian dishes by performing some quick minigames. Simple, but charming! The rest of the time you're off killing some ghoulies that look like mutated fruit and veggies, with the occasional fungus-possessed hog and, uh, haunted statues? I think?

I'm also quite pleased about two points made on the game's Steam page. First is the content description: "This game features cartoon violence, sensitive political themes set in a fictional world, and depictions of an oppressive government committing crimes against its citizens." There is clearly a romantic quality to the game and I'd be worried if it didn't acknowledge any of the political context of the decades preceding.

The other line reads, "Every sound effect, musical note, design decision, and line of code is human-made. Because this game is about human relationships and delicious food – and that’s not a story we would ever trust AI to tell." Thank the lord! Right now there's no release date attached to The Snackbar at the End of the World, unsurprising given it was only announced this week. But while we all wait for a date, you could perhaps join me in throwing it a wishlist on Steam.

title: Pinot Noir: Inside the Criminal Gangs Making Fake Wine
author: Peter Rubin
content:
While wine fraud has been around for nearly 150 years, it exploded around the turn of the century, with enterprising counterfeiters drawn by high margins and relatively low risk. Now, though, with the highest-end manufacturers upping their game, would-be forgers are looking at more moderately priced targets; they’ve even come for mass-market brands like Yellow Tail. For 1843, William Ralston uncorks the zero-somm game.

Other popular anti-counterfeiting techniques used by high-end wineries include manufacturing proprietary bottle shapes and micro-printing, where text and patterns are printed at a scale visible only under magnification. (I was shown a bottle of 2009 Le Pin, a fine Bordeaux wine, where the names of the winery owner’s children had been micro-printed repeatedly between two thin red lines on its front label.) Some wineries have adopted advanced security measures, incorporating features like holograms, individualised digital tracking codes and inks that change colour when tilted. Pétrus, a Bordeaux winery which produces only 30,000 bottles a year, uses inks custom-made by the same company that produces the ones used on American dollar bills.

title: When Anesthesia Goes Wrong
author: Seyward Darby
content:
A teenage boy went into surgery for a broken arm and emerged with brain damage. His mother was determined to figure out what had happened. Turns out, he wasn’t the only young person adversely affected by anesthesia. A riveting medical mystery from Sarah Zhang:

Over the years, Yaremy had talked with colleagues in Venezuela about Uli so relentlessly that word sometimes came back to her of similar cases: nearly always kids, nearly always after routine surgery. An introvert by nature, Yaremy had to learn to badger anyone and everyone for a useful crumb of information.

She began running down some of these rumors: The wife of the son of a friend knew a neurologist who knew an anesthesiologist who knew of a boy who had fallen ill after surgery on a broken forearm. He became patient four. Patient five was the boy whose mother she’d met picking up Botox in Caracas. A physical therapist told her about a boy who’d had cleft-lip surgery—patient six. An old friend from medical school, an anesthesiologist, had examined a boy who developed symptoms after surgery for a cochlear implant. The friend had once been skeptical of Yaremy’s theory, but now he helped her gather data. This boy became the seventh and final patient in the study. . . . A haunting pattern appeared in the cases she was able to pull together. All seven patients in the study had received sevoflurane. Most of them could trace their maternal relatives to Carabobo; Yaremy’s own maternal grandmother was from the state. And all seven had the same T-to-C mutation.

title: “Club Kid” and the New Fatherhood
author: @NewYorker
content:
The archetype of the father onscreen has come a long way from the patriarchs of the postwar era. The new film “Club Kid” joins a wave of recent works that interrogate what we want from dads today—in art and in life.

November 12, 2026

Download a transcript.

Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen

Sign up to receive our weekly cultural-recommendations newsletter.

The protagonist of the new film “Club Kid” never meant to become a dad. Peter, played by Jordan Firstman, who also wrote and directed the film, is a gay party promoter whose years in the New York club scene are finally catching up with him. When his ten-year-old biological son unexpectedly comes into the picture, Peter is forced to reckon with his new role in life. On this episode of Critics at Large, Vinson Cunningham, Naomi Fry, and Alexandra Schwartz consider how depictions of fatherhood in the culture have evolved over time. After the women’s-liberation movement, postwar Don Draper-esque patriarchs gave way to a cohort of lovable sitcom dunces, laying the groundwork for the ultimate satire of American fatherhood: Homer Simpson. Today, dads seem to be more pals than patriarchs. Since 1965, partnered American fathers have nearly quadrupled the time they spend with their kids, resulting in a host of new ideas about what a dad is and how to be a good one. Amid seismic cultural shifts, one thing remains unchanged: paternal figures loom large in our lives, and yet there’s no such thing as a perfect dad. “Once you’re a parent, the performance of the role . . . it’s like nobody can actually inhabit it,” Cunningham says. “You think of the father as the person who ruined you or the person who saves you. And of course, you’re always both.”

title: How an Unlikely Charles de Gaulle Bio-Pic Conquered France
author: @NewYorker
content:
Bringing the French general to the big screen has historically been a fraught enterprise. Antonin Baudry says that his two-part epic succeeded because it “managed to crack the character.”

November 12, 2026

Simon Abkarian in “De Gaulle,” from 2026.Photograph courtesy of Samuel Goldwyn Films

In the summer of 1942, a cash-strapped William Faulkner signed on to work at Warner Bros. as a screenwriter, earning three hundred dollars a week. His first task was to whip up a biographical treatment of General Charles de Gaulle, leading the Free French government from exile in London. Provisionally titled “The De Gaulle Story,” the project was intended as hagiography—explicitly so, as President Franklin Roosevelt had proposed the idea to Jack Warner, hoping to boost de Gaulle’s credibility with the American public. Faulkner gave the gig his best shot, producing some twelve hundred pages and entertaining fussy notes from French consultants. (A memo titled “Observations on Inexact Details” cautioned, “In a cafe in France one does not play dominos but cards or billiard.”) Ultimately, Faulkner found his protagonist so hard to pin down that he purged the bio from the bio-pic, instructing a colleague, “Let’s dispense with General de Gaulle as a living character in the story.” The script was soon relegated to oblivion.

Churchills and Roosevelts—not to mention Hitlers—abound in cinema, but, even in France, bringing de Gaulle to the big screen has historically been a fraught enterprise. As the British historian Julian Jackson has written, postwar filmmakers strove to emphasize the collective nature of resistance rather than focussing on a single great man; yet, when de Gaulle returned to power in 1958, becoming President after more than a decade’s retirement from politics, it was with such command that, as Jackson puts it, “to dare to ask an actor to portray de Gaulle himself would have been an act of lèse-majesté.” (The director Réné Clément solved the problem by using archival footage whenever the General’s presence was required.) Pierre Schoendoerffer and Bertrand Tavernier both tried to make de Gaulle films and failed, the latter surely unhelped by his producer’s insistence that the lead character be played by Gérard Depardieu. Then there was the challenge of de Gaulle’s distinctive physiognomy. Such were the sensitivities surrounding him and his myth that a single actor—the towering, schnozzy, serviceably chinless Adrien Cayla-Legrand—maintained an effective monopoly on the role for decades. It wasn’t until 2020 that the first full-scale feature film devoted to the General, Gabriel Le Bomin’s “De Gaulle,” premièred in French theatres. It closed just ten days later, with COVID-19 advancing like the Panzerjäger-Abteilung 187.

This is all to say that Antonin Baudry knew what he was getting into when he signed on to co-write and direct the most ambitious, improbable de Gaulle movie yet: “La Bataille de Gaulle”—a two-part, five-plus-hour epic, based on Julian Jackson’s nine-hundred-page biography “A Certain Idea of France.” (The book's title alludes to the opening lines of de Gaulle’s own memoirs: “All my life, I have had a certain idea of France.”) The film captivated France this summer, and the first part opened last week in the U.S. Its timing has certainly been fortuitous, with France facing a Presidential election that may put the far right in power for the first time since the Vichy regime. But when we met recently, at a café in the Luxembourg Gardens, Baudry told me he believes that the film has resonated largely because of its human element. He looked chicly rumpled in cream trousers, a button-down, and white leather high-tops decorated with red lightning bolts. He said, of the filmmakers who preceded him, “I understood the malediction—none of them had dared and managed to crack the character.”

Baudry, who is fifty-one, began his career far from the moving image, studying math before earning degrees in engineering and literature from France’s arch-prestigious grandes écoles. (He managed to slip in a film-studies minor, with a thesis on Wong Kar-wai.) After graduating, he entered the French diplomatic corps, where he worked as a speechwriter to the Foreign Minister at the time, Dominique de Villepin, and at least partially authored his famous speech at the United Nations, opposing the Iraq War. After that, he pseudonymously co-wrote a graphic novel called “Quai d’Orsay,” after the seat of the foreign ministry. The book—a juicy look at the inner workings of foreign-policymaking—was a hit, selling more than sixty thousand copies of its first edition. Having proved himself as a sort of beast of the French establishment, devouring the competition in every arena he entered, Baudry volunteered to co-write a film adaptation. Then he decided he wanted to be a director. Casual. So he wangled a meeting with Jérôme Seydoux, the chairman of Pathé film company, and persuaded him to finance a nuclear-submarine thriller called “Chant du Loup,” which premièred in 2019 to warm reviews and respectable takings.

For the de Gaulle project, Pathé gave Baudry carte blanche and an initial seventy-five million euros, an unheard-of budget for a French production. (The film was called “La Bataille de Gaulle” in France but is known as “De Gaulle” in the U.S.) It focusses on the critical years of 1940 to 1944, beginning, in Part 1, with de Gaulle refusing to join the collaborationist Vichy government and ending, in Part 2, with his triumphant return from exile during the Liberation of Paris. Baudry had a breakthrough when he and his co-writer, Bérénice Vila, who is also his wife, started thinking about de Gaulle as a figure spiritually not of the mid-century but of the Middle Ages. “I realized that de Gaulle was a modern Don Quixote,” Baudry recalled, citing the General’s “denial, his stubbornness, his readiness to die rather than admitting the unbearable reality that France had capitulated.” Once the notion of de Gaulle as a knight-errant had clicked, Baudry and Vila came up with a tactic to alleviate the pressure of his legend: as they wrote, they called their hero “Robert” instead of “Charles.” They emphasized the initial lostness of his cause: a mad band of marginals, holding on to France out of unaccountable faith, rather than a reasonable chance of wresting control from Vichy. By that point, Baudry recalled, “I had my character in my veins, and I was going to make these films.”

For the title role, Baudry cast Simon Abkarian, an actor best known for his work on the stage. The film took a hundred and fifty gruelling days to shoot, with reports of delays, quarrels, and a generally trying atmosphere leaking from sets in Paris and Cherbourg. Several months into filming, some twenty crew members quit, including the first assistant director and the director of photography. After filming finally wrapped, in 2024, post-production took more than a year, and Part 1 missed an anticipated release date in 2025. When it finally premièred, in May, at Cannes, reviews were mostly positive. Les Cahiers du Cinema criticized its formal “heavy-handedness” and its “idealized vision” of France, but critics in Le Monde and Le Figaro loved it. “De Gaulle” had won a battle, but it had not won the war.

The first installment hit French theatres in June, to dismal ticket sales. Baudry, meanwhile, was M.I.A., still editing the sound for Part 2. “I honestly didn’t give a shit about the noise outside the mixing room,” he recalled. The film’s producers, hoping for a turnaround, moved up the release of the second installment to coincide with la Fête du Cinema, a nationwide promotion offering discounted tickets. (The films’ full titles—“La Bataille de Gaulle: L’Âge de Fer” and “La Bataille de Gaulle: J’Écris Ton Nom”—were unwieldy enough to cause at least one moviegoer, yours truly, to accidentally see the second part first.) Executives overhauled the marketing campaign. Seydoux told me, “We had a crisis meeting, and I said, ‘We have a rifle with only two shots.’ ”

Then came a third, lucky blast—record-breaking heat, which sent people flocking to the cinema, one of the only reliable places to find air-conditioning. By its fourth week in theatres, “La Bataille de Gaulle” had seen admissions surge by seventy per cent. Word-of-mouth took over, and, suddenly, “La Bataille de Gaulle” was a sensation. I heard chatter about it, in the course of a few days, from both a government minister and my boxing coach. “It’s French panache!” Le Parisien crowed, heralding “a fiasco turned triumph.” The trajectory was almost embarrassingly de Gaullian: a crazy project, flailing and discounted, mounting a gritty comeback that would subsequently be treated as inevitable.

In late September, Jérôme Seydoux was sitting in an orange chair at a huge circular conference table on the top floor of Pathé Palace, his company’s Paris headquarters. He has piercing blue eyes and the plain confidence of a man born to industrial wealth—his mother was a member of the Schlumberger oil dynasty—who managed to conquer another field completely. (He is also grandfather to the actor Léa Seydoux.) At ninety-two, he is something of a cross between Louis B. Mayer and Willy Wonka, confecting France’s major films according to a proprietary formula of market savvy and personal conviction.

Seydoux and Baudry like to say that the “De Gaulle” project took shape out of serendipity: over lunch, they discovered that they were both reading the Julian Jackson biography. But in a way Seydoux has been preparing for much longer to make such a film. “I am an old man, and the story, to some extent, is the story of my life,” he admitted. Seydoux witnessed firsthand the Liberation of Paris, in August of 1944. “We tried to go to the Champs-Élysées, but we didn’t make it, because we were crossing the Tuileries and there were people shooting on the Rue de Rivoli,” he recalled. “The soldiers advised my mother to have us all go under a truck to be protected.” Another day, he and his sister were forbidden to go outside, but they snuck out and saw a German tank. “Kids were able to move because nobody would stop them,” he said.

Making a wildly expensive diptych about a long-dead, famously wooden statesman was a gamble, surely, but it conformed to a strategy that Seydoux has pursued to success in recent years,. This involves taking canonical French stories and turning them into “grandes fresques historiques,” the kind of lavish historical epics at which Hollywood once excelled in the nineteen-fifties and sixties. The movies are old-fashioned, and they are expensive, but they have proved adept at drawing big, cross-generational crowds to physical theatres. Pathé’s “The Three Musketeers: D’Artagnan” was the third-highest-grossing French film of 2023; the next year, its “The Count of Monte Cristo” took second place. “It’s this sort of instinctive I.P.,” the film critic Jordan Mintzer told me. “We have Marvel. They have Dumas.” The advantage of resurrecting a wartime superhero is that the world he saves is our own, though “De Gaulle” would have been a very different proposition if it had followed its protagonist into the years of the Algerian War, decolonization, and student revolt.

Baudry has said that he approached the film from another kind of decolonial perspective—that of a French director “breaking the Atlanticist taboo” and liberating his national history from the clutch of the American cultural empire. He spent years living in the U.S. (where he created Albertine, the French cultural center in Manhattan), and when he came back to France he found “a country that was mentally colonized,” as he told Le Monde. “I saw advertisements in public spaces written in broken English that even Americans wouldn’t have understood.” His de Gaulle is difficult, not because he is a comedy Frenchman but because he is a steadfast believer in the near-hopeless cause of maintaining the sovereignty of la Fraaaaaahnce. (Abkarian’s enunciation is the stuff of epic earworms.) “I embody everything the Americans detest,” de Gaulle once said. “I am weak, and I stand my ground.” In the film, he also says borderline delusional stuff such as, “Mosquitoes don’t bite General de Gaulle!” In the next scene, he’s in bed with malaria. Baudry explained, of the General’s almost mystical self-belief, “You have to be passionate. If you’re reasonable, you leave.”

Roosevelt, played by Campbell Scott, is a far more sour, transactional figure than the morally driven humanitarian we know from American history books. Churchill (Simon Russell Beale) waffles and feints as much as he blusters. Baudry told me, “This is the first time we’re seeing this full history through our own lens.” Call it a reverse Pepé Le Pew, flattening Anglo-American icons to give some space not only to de Gaulle but to his internal antagonists and allies and to the French people themselves. Niels Schneider’s sensational performance makes you long for a spinoff two-part, five-hour bio-pic of the Free French general Philippe Leclerc. Baudry’s dramatization of the Germans' violent crackdown on dozens of mostly young, civilian protesters on November 11, 1940, incorporating real live archival footage, is among the most moving set pieces I’ve seen. And nobody who has seen this film will ever forget the Battle of Bir-Hakeim.

There are many ironies to “De Gaulle”—a great-man bio-pic distinguished by its ensemble cast; an anti-American, or at least American-agnostic, film done in high Hollywood style. But its biggest contradiction might be the fact that it is both avowedly antifascist and profoundly patriotic, a film about resistance that could be seen as almost reactionary in its insistence on the purity of de Gaulle and his cause. During our coffee, I asked Baudry whether he’d had any reservations about making a movie that is so overtly, even unfashionably proud of France. He answered in a sidelong way, saying that he hadn’t anticipated the powerful frissons of pride that many moviegoers had reported feeling. Weeks later, I received a long text: “I keep thinking about our exchange in the Luxembourg Garden,” it began. “I don’t want to sound naïve on this,” Baudry wrote. Part of the problem, he said, was that “the far-right has managed to monopolize patriotism,” confiscating “our flag and our pride.” He brought up American exceptionalism, and said that “De Gaulle” does not try to argue for a French version. “It doesn’t say that the French are better than the Spanish, the British, the Americans,” he said. “It just shows people trying to save their country which is France and which they love.”

“Why now?” is an irksome question to impose on an artist, but with Europe struggling to assert itself against an increasingly aggressive American hegemon, and people all over the world searching for models of resistance against autocratic regimes, Baudry is not oblivious to the film’s broader resonances. “I thought to myself, It’s Trump-Zelensky!” he told Le Grand Continent, of a scene in which Roosevelt and de Gaulle face off at the Anfa Hotel, in Casablanca, in 1943. Baudry told me that the current political situation put him in mind of the words of Edward Grey, the British Foreign Secretary in 1914: “The lamps are going out all over Europe, we shall not see them lit again in our life-time.” He continued, “That was true, and that’s a little bit what we’re fearing now.” “De Gaulle” joins a slew of other recent French movies about the Second World War, including “Notre Salut,” a drama by Emmanuel Marre about his collaborationist great-grandfather, and a starry bio-pic of the French Resistance leader Jean Moulin. But “De Gaulle,” like its hero, stands out for its willingness to be true to itself, and even a little weird. Baudry brought up Don Quixote again. “A knight devoted to his lady isn’t necessarily convinced that she is technically more beautiful than, say, the king’s wife,” he told me. “He just thinks she’s perfect, and he’ll die for her any time if needed.” It’s a certain idea about a certain idea. ♦

An earlier version of this article inaccurately described the dramatization of the November 11, 1940, civilian crackdown.

title: When Idaho Banned Abortion, OB-GYNs Fled. The Doctors Who Stayed Are Cracking.
author: Seyward Darby
content:
Last week, voters in Idaho rejected a measure that would have restored the right to terminate a pregnancy up to the point of fetal viability. (The state’s abortion ban went into effect after Roe v. Wade was overturned.) It’s a devastating blow for Idaho’s women and obstetricians—those who are still practicing, that is. More than one-third of the state’s OBGYNs are no longer doing obstetrics; many have moved or retired. Today, half of Idaho’s counties do not have a practicing obstetrician. Lisa Lerer spends time with some of the state’s remaining reproductive health doctors, who are just trying to keep their heads above water:

Parker reached into her patient’s abdomen and gently jiggled and wiggled with her hands, trying to separate the spongy red disc from the uterine wall, as she had done many times before in her practice as a family-medicine doctor with a specialization in high-risk obstetrics. The organ didn’t budge. Within minutes, Parker knew what she was facing: a placenta accreta, a dangerous complication in which the placenta grows into the uterine wall.

With her hands still in her patient’s open abdomen, Parker asked her nurse to call the obstetricians. The nurse held the phone to Parker’s ear as she received the news: The OB working that morning was in Washington and would be delayed. Her patient would have to wait, lying on the surgical table with her body cut open.

More stories about reproductive rights

“Since last October, the families of every fallen soldier have been offered post-mortem sperm retrieval.”

title: The Long-Awaited Rise of Tinashe
author: @NewYorker
content:
In 2014, a twenty-year-old singer named Tinashe released a steamy track called “2 On,” which proved to be extremely popular and a little bit misleading. The song didn’t top the pop chart, but new listeners kept finding it, and then coming back to it; on Spotify, it has been streamed more than eight hundred million times. Over a low-slung hip-hop beat, Tinashe sings, “I love to get 2 on,” and then she explains what that means: “Get faded, turn up, bruh, pour it on up till I can’t even think no more / Get ratchet, go dumb, then go more dumb, then we can keep it lit, let’s roll.” Her delivery is seductive enough to make the two lines rhyme, and to make the anatomically specific guest verse, from the rapper ScHoolboy Q, seem entirely appropriate. Tinashe was brought up in show business, having worked as a child actor and as a member of a girl group, the Stunners, whose addition to the canon of bubblegum pop was a playfully robotic song called, fittingly, “Bubblegum.” The success of “2 On” seemed to herald her arrival as a grownup R. & B. hitmaker, ready to take her place among the genre’s gyrating headliners, with songs about hookups, heartbreaks, and nights out that were either unforgettable or unrememberable.

In fact, the singer who made her name promising to “go dumb” turned out to be an uncommonly thoughtful and careful musician, turning out meticulously crafted songs that earned her a small army of fans convinced that it should be a big army. Tinashe struggled with her record company, RCA, which at one point released an earnest love song, “Flame,” which she evidently did not consider her best work. (“I cried for two days when they told me I had to put that song out as a single,” she later said.) For a while, she distributed her music independently, and then she joined Atlantic Records, which in September issued “Popstar”; the record could be considered Tinashe’s thirteenth release, if we count mixtapes and mini-albums. “Popstar” is a collection of songs that is partly about the twelve collections that preceded it—about, that is, the gruelling process of trying to become a pop star. Tinashe has said that one song, “Empty Stadium,” is based on a recurring nightmare about being trapped onstage with no audience and no exit. “I put the work in, and I waited / Don’t wanna die underrated,” she sings, and there’s no telling whether this is part of the same dream, or her wide-awake reaction.

Happily, “Popstar” is a riotously good time, and also, it seems, a self-fulfilling prophecy. It débuted at No. 6 on the Billboard album chart, putting Tinashe in the Top Ten for the first time in her long career. On a recent Saturday night, she turned up at Brooklyn Paramount to celebrate, performing a sold-out show for about twenty-eight hundred fans, many of whom seemed as if they had been waiting for this moment even longer than she had. She appeared flanked by four dancers dressed, from the waist up, as paparazzi: black jackets, flashing cameras, no pants. She was singing the album’s titular song, asking, “Tell me, is it everything you thought it’d be?” On the record, the beat drops out, leaving Tinashe alone with stacked echoes of her own voice, which suggest that the answer is no. But for more than an hour in Brooklyn, the crowd left no room for misgivings, hollering loudest for the sassiest lyrics, and whooping every time Tinashe or one of her dancers lifted a leg or dropped a backside. A few days later, she got an endorsement from the Swedish singer Robyn, who incorporated part of “Popstar” into a live performance on BBC Radio 1. Robyn is probably the patron saint of cult-favorite pop stars, a designation that seems much less paradoxical than it once did, thanks to the rise of singers like Tinashe, who appear to thrive in their own cultural galaxies, whether or not they ever cross over into ours.

In 2014, at the dawn of her career, Tinashe told an interviewer that her music was “rooted in a place of R. & B.,” and many of her early tracks have beats that are stately and restrained enough to let her carve out memorable vocal lines, enriched by well-chosen harmonies and ad-libs. The song “Nasty,” from 2024, marked a commercial resurgence, inspiring millions of TikTok videos, some of which showed users lip-synching the question Tinashe poses: “Is somebody gonna match my freak?” Part of what made the line work was the trancelike way she delivered it, as if she weren’t sure what had come over her; eerie keyboards and a ghostly beat echoed the unsettled mood. “No Broke Boys,” her other recent hit, pulled off a similar trick, pairing feisty lyrics with incongruously pensive music. Last year, the producer known as Disco Lines remixed it, building a muscular house track around Tinashe’s taunting refrain: “No broke boys, no new friends.” It became one of the year’s biggest dance tracks and has been streamed about a billion times on Spotify—drawing in, no doubt, plenty of listeners who knew nothing about Tinashe’s trajectory, even as they were helping to change it.

One of the defining qualities of pop stardom is that it is bigger than music: hit songs help create vivid personas and vice versa, and today it is easier than ever to follow the semiprivate lives of public people. Tinashe, though, is more self-contained. She is poised and polite, offering fans no personal details to match the decadence and drama in her lyrics. During a recent conversation with Ricky Reed, who served as an executive producer of “Popstar,” Tinashe dissected “Nasty” with a music nerd’s exactitude. “There was a really interesting moment where we found that juxtaposition between, like, the minor chords and the major chords,” she recalled. (Once, when a radio host asked her to name celebrities beginning with the letter “T,” she started with Tori Amos, the melodically expansive singer-songwriter.) These days, Tinashe seems to be deëmphasizing R. & B., perhaps in keeping with her ambitions; during a recent interview, she said, “I always saw myself as a pop artist.” On the new album, her voice is smaller and the percussion is brawnier than before. She sounds enviably unhurried when she coos, “I know that I’m a superstar,” even though the drums are hammering away at around a hundred and thirty-six beats per minute, which is nearly as fast as pop music can get without turning into something else.

Onstage in Brooklyn, Tinashe said almost nothing to the crowd besides “Thank you so much”—confident, perhaps, that the precision of her vocal lines and the prerecorded backing tracks would tell the audience everything it needed to know, and that people would arrive with plenty of their own unhinged energy. Pop stardom is a collaborative project, well suited to the social-media era, and this makes it easier for fans to participate, competing to express their enthusiasm in maximally hyperbolic terms. (When someone on X asked for an example of a historical event so glorious that it could be considered “the Opposite of 9/11,” a fan proposed February 6, 1993: the day Tinashe was born.) The crowd at Brooklyn Paramount was full of Black women and gay men, who have long been among Tinashe’s most voluble supporters, and when it came time to perform “Melatonin,” the new album’s raucous highlight, she brought fans onstage for a dance party, with men and women equally eager to twerk for their idol. When the show was over, she headed across the bridge for a d.j. set at a Manhattan night club, but some of the fans stayed put, continuing the dance party out on the sidewalk. For at least a moment, Tinashe’s world and the real world seemed like the same place.

How long will stylized, self-conscious pop music remain in vogue? The wave crested in 2024, when Charli XCX—after years of niche fame—conquered the world with “Brat,” a brilliant meta-pop opus. Earlier this year, Charli seemed to announce a cultural shift when she released a song called “Rock Music,” declaring, “I think the dance floor is dead / So now we’re making ro-o-o-ock music,” dragging out the word as if she were stifling a yawn. And yet the pop era has endured. A playfully obnoxious pop auteur named Slayyyter has lately ascended to stardom; she is booked to play Madison Square Garden next summer. And JADE, a former member of the British girl group Little Mix, currently has a delayed-reaction hit with “Angel of My Dreams,” a 2024 song that perfectly evokes a bygone era of bombastic Euro-pop, morphing from a ballad into a dance track and back again. (It was the soundtrack to Kylie Jenner’s star turn at last month’s Victoria’s Secret fashion show.)

It also seems clear that “pop,” always a nebulous term, is evolving. In Mexico, an emerging singer named FLVCKKA (pronounced “flaca”) is using sparkling keyboards and up-tempo rhythms to create addictive hybrids that can sound simultaneously dreamy and streetwise. On her new album, “Hypercorridos Vol. 1,” FLVCKKA marries the giddy sensibility of hyper-pop with the tenacious spirit of Mexican corridos, ballads that tend toward the extremes of triumph and tragedy. The record includes “Si No Contestas,” a duet with Marcos Villalobos that is not as playful as it might seem: it turns out that the lovers trading promises also happen to be carrying guns. On the album cover, FLVCKKA is surrounded by scantily dressed friends and heavily armed police officers: a pop star in her own mind, and maybe—with a lot of work and a bit of luck—elsewhere, too. ♦
